attachments.origin_landmark: external occipital protuberance, nuchal ligament, spinous processes C7-T12
attachments.insertion_landmark: spine of scapula, acromion, lateral clavicle

actions: upper+lower parts together upwardly rotate the scapula (essential for full overhead arm elevation)

functional_compartments.name: Upper (descending) part
functional_compartments.function_note: Fibers run inferolaterally from occiput/upper cervical spine to the lateral clavicle/acromion; classically described as elevating the scapula, though Johnson et al.'s dissection study argues this transverse-ish fiber orientation contributes to scapular rotation mainly once rotation (driven by lower trapezius + serratus anterior) is already underway, rather than acting as a simple independent elevator.
functional_compartments.source: Johnson G, Bogduk N, Nowitzke A, House D (1994) Clin Biomech 9(1):44-50 -- dissection/volumetric study of trapezius's 3 fiber regions; the paper's own finding is more nuanced than the popular textbook summary -- it explicitly argues the essentially transverse orientation of the upper and middle fibers 'precludes any action as elevators of the scapula as commonly depicted,' proposing instead a coupled mechanism where the lower fibers fix the scapula's medial border isometrically so serratus anterior can rotate it, with upper fibers contributing to rotation only once it is already underway. The simple 'upper=elevator/middle=retractor/lower=depressor, upper+lower=force couple' model is standard simplified teaching (Gray's/Kenhub level), not this paper's own conclusion (corrected from an earlier draft that attributed the simplified model directly to this paper -- caught by adversarial fact-check, see docs/VERIFICATION.md)

functional_compartments.name: Middle (transverse) part
functional_compartments.function_note: Fibers run purely transversely (horizontally) from thoracic spinous processes to the acromion/scapular spine; the muscle's pure retractor component.
functional_compartments.source: Johnson G, Bogduk N, Nowitzke A, House D (1994) Clin Biomech 9(1):44-50 -- dissection/volumetric study of trapezius's 3 fiber regions; the paper's own finding is more nuanced than the popular textbook summary -- it explicitly argues the essentially transverse orientation of the upper and middle fibers 'precludes any action as elevators of the scapula as commonly depicted,' proposing instead a coupled mechanism where the lower fibers fix the scapula's medial border isometrically so serratus anterior can rotate it, with upper fibers contributing to rotation only once it is already underway. The simple 'upper=elevator/middle=retractor/lower=depressor, upper+lower=force couple' model is standard simplified teaching (Gray's/Kenhub level), not this paper's own conclusion (corrected from an earlier draft that attributed the simplified model directly to this paper -- caught by adversarial fact-check, see docs/VERIFICATION.md)

functional_compartments.name: Lower (ascending) part
functional_compartments.function_note: Fibers run superolaterally from lower thoracic spinous processes to the medial scapular spine; the standard teaching model describes this depressing the scapula and, paired with the upper part, forming a force couple producing upward rotation -- though per Johnson et al.'s dissection findings, the more precise mechanism is that the lower fibers isometrically fix the scapula's medial border so serratus anterior can drive the actual rotation. Either way, a genuine 3-way fiber-direction functional split within one named muscle.
